werk/the-byrds-fifth-dimension.text:
Fifth Dimension was released on 18 July 1966 as the Byrds' third album. In December 1965 the band recorded Eight Miles High and Why at RCA Studios, but Columbia refused to release them because they had not been recorded in its own studio. Both songs were re-recorded under producer Allen Stanton, who had succeeded Terry Melcher. Shortly afterwards chief songwriter Gene Clark left the group. As a result Jim McGuinn and David Crosby began to write more themselves.

Eight Miles High blends McGuinn's guitar playing, influenced by John Coltrane, with raga structures inspired by the Indian classical music of Ravi Shankar. The song was important for the transition from folk rock to psychedelia. The album has four covers and an instrumental piece and was called uneven, and it was the first without a song by Bob Dylan. Even so it was seen as their most experimental record up to that point, and critics regard it as influential for the emergence of psychedelic rock.
werk/the-byrds-fifth-dimension.listen: Listen to Eight Miles High and notice how McGuinn's guitar, inspired by Coltrane, winds its way over the vocals.

werk/the-byrds-mr-tambourine-man.text:
The Byrds came out of the Los Angeles folk scene. In January 1965 they recorded Bob Dylan's Mr. Tambourine Man as their debut single. Producer Terry Melcher brought in session musicians, so that only guitarist Jim McGuinn himself played on it. For the album the band was allowed to play the accompaniment itself; recording was finished on 22 April 1965.

The record consists of folk songs, mostly by Dylan, and original work by singer Gene Clark, such as I'll Feel a Whole Lot Better. The characteristic sound is McGuinn's jangling twelve-string Rickenbacker, combined with multi-part harmony singing. In this way the band fused folk, a British beat and an electric rock beat. The album helped to make the folk rock movement known. The single reached number 1 in the United States and the United Kingdom, and according to critics it was the first serious American challenge to the Beatles and the other British bands.
werk/the-byrds-mr-tambourine-man.listen: Listen to the twelve-string guitar in Mr. Tambourine Man, which colours the melody, and to the several voices singing together.

werk/the-byrds-sweetheart-of-the-rodeo.text:
Sweetheart of the Rodeo was released in August 1968 on Columbia Records. Roger McGuinn first wanted to make a double album about the history of American popular music, but the young Gram Parsons, who joined the band in February 1968, persuaded him and Chris Hillman to make a pure country record. The recording was divided between Nashville and Los Angeles, with session musicians such as Lloyd Green, John Hartford and Clarence White. By the time the album came out, Parsons had already left the group again.

The repertoire includes two Dylan songs from his Basement Tapes, You Ain't Goin' Nowhere and Nothing Was Delivered, alongside classic country songs such as I Am a Pilgrim. Parsons brought Hickory Wind. In Nashville the group was booed as hippies at the Grand Ole Opry. Commercially it was their least successful album up to that point, but today it is regarded as an influential country rock record.
werk/the-byrds-sweetheart-of-the-rodeo.listen: Listen to Hickory Wind and notice the pedal steel guitar and the soft singing. Can you hear how country takes over the sound of a rock group here?

werk/the-byrds-the-notorious-byrd-brothe.text:
The Notorious Byrd Brothers was released on 15 January 1968 on Columbia Records. The recording sessions in the second half of 1967, again with producer Gary Usher, were marked by quarrels. David Crosby was fired in October, drummer Michael Clarke left the sessions halfway through and Gene Clark returned for three weeks. By the end of the process only Roger McGuinn and Chris Hillman remained.

Even so the album often sounds soft and floating. The Byrds blended folk rock, country, psychedelia and jazz and used phasing and rotating speakers. It is one of the first rock albums with a Moog synthesizer, and for the first time pedal steel guitar was heard. The album opens with Artificial Energy, about the dark side of amphetamine, with a hefty horn section. It sold modestly, especially in America, but was praised by critics and is now regarded as one of their best albums.
werk/the-byrds-the-notorious-byrd-brothe.listen: Listen to Space Odyssey and notice the Moog synthesizer. Can you hear how those electronic sounds make a new sound in a folk rock band?

werk/the-byrds-turn-turn-turn.text:
After the success of their debut album and the hit Mr. Tambourine Man, the Byrds went into Columbia Studios in Hollywood on 28 June 1965 to record a follow-up. A version of Bob Dylan's It's All Over Now, Baby Blue was rejected, and in the end the group chose Turn! Turn! Turn!, Pete Seeger's adaptation of text from the Book of Ecclesiastes. The song took them back to number one on the American Hot 100.

The album sounds like its predecessor: folk rock with multi-part harmony singing and Jim McGuinn's clear twelve-string Rickenbacker. Besides Dylan covers such as The Times They Are a-Changin' and Lay Down Your Weary Tune, Gene Clark still wrote the most original material, but McGuinn wrote more and David Crosby received his first writing credit. The atmosphere was tense. Afterwards producer Terry Melcher had to leave, and in early 1966 Clark left the group.
werk/the-byrds-turn-turn-turn.listen: Listen to Turn! Turn! Turn! (To Everything There Is a Season) and notice how the guitar and the stacked vocal harmonies together make a light, ringing sound beneath a Bible text.

werk/the-byrds-younger-than-yesterday.text:
Younger Than Yesterday was released on 6 February 1967 on Columbia Records and was the Byrds' fourth album. Gene Clark was gone, the group's popularity was declining, and with new producer Gary Usher the album was recorded in eleven days at Columbia Studios in Hollywood. The group experimented with horns, reversed tape effects and an electronic oscillator.

Bassist Chris Hillman came to the fore for the first time as a singer and writer, and two of his songs point ahead to country rock. The album opens with So You Want to Be a Rock 'n' Roll Star, a mocking song with a trumpet solo by Hugh Masekela and the sound of screaming fans. C.T.A.-102 speculates about extraterrestrial life. At the time the album was largely ignored, but critical appreciation grew, and today it is regarded as one of the group's best.
werk/the-byrds-younger-than-yesterday.listen: Listen to So You Want to Be a Rock 'n' Roll Star and notice the trumpet and the screaming in the background. Can you hear how the lyrics poke fun at the pop world?

werk/the-chemical-brothers-come-with-us.text:
Come with Us is the fourth studio album by the Chemical Brothers and was released on 28 January 2002. After the world tour for Surrender, which lasted until the summer of 2000, the duo began work on new material. Recording took eighteen months. They experimented with new equipment, such as a Parker MIDI Fly guitar, and began with string arpeggios, hard MIDI notes and loose drum sounds. Richard Ashcroft and Beth Orton can be heard as guest vocalists.

It Began in Afrika started out as the club test Electronic Battle Weapon 5 and, together with Star Guitar, reached number 8 in the UK singles chart. Galaxy Bounce became known in the summer of 2001 through the soundtrack of Lara Croft: Tomb Raider. The album entered at number 1 in the United Kingdom, the third in a row. AllMusic felt that after Surrender, full of guest stars, the duo was getting down to business again.
werk/the-chemical-brothers-come-with-us.listen: Listen to It Began in Afrika, in the six-minute album version, and notice how the track flows into Galaxy Bounce.

werk/the-chemical-brothers-dig-your-own-.text:
Dig Your Own Hole is the second album by The Chemical Brothers, recorded between 1996 and 1997. The duo already had a successful debut behind them, Exit Planet Dust, and had moved from Junior Boy's Own to Virgin. Two tracks first appeared as promo records for DJs, to try them out in the clubs. Noel Gallagher of Oasis wrote a lyric for an instrumental he was given: that became Setting Sun, a number one in the United Kingdom.

The record uses samples of Schoolly D and Lothar and the Hand People, among others. Block Rockin' Beats also became a number one, and the album went to the top of the UK chart. Critics praised the way it removed the opposition between rock and techno. Rolling Stone and Spin included it in their lists of the best albums of the 1990s.
werk/the-chemical-brothers-dig-your-own-.listen: Listen to Noel Gallagher's vocals over the electronic music in Setting Sun. Notice how rock and dance come together in one song.

werk/the-chemical-brothers-exit-planet-d.text:
Exit Planet Dust was the British duo's debut, released in 1995. Recording ran from August to November 1994. Before that, Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons had already been DJing and making remixes, under the name Dust Brothers. An American production duo of the same name threatened legal action, and so it became The Chemical Brothers. The album title refers to that change of name. The first six tracks run into one another like a medley. They include Leave Home, Chemical Beats and Song to the Siren, which was recorded live in a London club.

The sound is big and bombastic, with screaming guitar samples and sirens. Leave Home and Life Is Sweet became singles. The press was enthusiastic: NME praised the raw, rule-breaking music, and AllMusic called it one of the few European post-techno records to gain a foothold in the United States. The album was later included in the book 1001 Albums You Must Hear Before You Die.
werk/the-chemical-brothers-exit-planet-d.listen: Listen to Leave Home and notice how the track opens with a short Kraftwerk sample before the heavy beat takes over.

werk/the-chemical-brothers-push-the-butt.text:
Push the Button is the fifth album by the Chemical Brothers and was released in January 2005. It received mostly good reviews and in January 2006 won a Grammy for Best Electronic/Dance Album. The British BPI certified it gold as early as 28 January 2005.

Galvanize was the first single, with Q-Tip as vocalist, and reached number 3 in the UK singles chart. The track contains a sample of Najat Aatabou. Believe reached number 18 and The Boxer number 41. BBC Music wrote that the duo returned with a rebellious rock record that blows away all stylistic boundaries. Complex was more critical and called it a hardly memorable project. As promotion the digital EP Live 05, recorded on the 2005 tour, was also released.
werk/the-chemical-brothers-push-the-butt.listen: Listen to Galvanize and notice Q-Tip's voice over the duo's electronic sounds.

werk/the-chi-lites-give-it-away.text:
Give It Away is the debut album by the American soul group The Chi-Lites. It was released in 1969 on the label Brunswick and was produced by Carl Davis and lead singer Eugene Record. It contains seven original songs and four covers: three Motown songs and The Twelfth of Never.

The album was well received and sold reasonably, especially in the R&B market, where it reached number 16. Five singles were released from it, four of which reached the R&B top 50 and two the Billboard Hot 100. The title song did best, with a tenth place on the R&B chart: the group's first top hit. In 2004 British television viewers heard the song What Do I Wish For in an advertisement for the fast-food chain KFC.
werk/the-chi-lites-give-it-away.listen: Listen to Give It Away, the group's first top ten hit on the R&B chart, and notice the voice of lead singer Eugene Record.

werk/the-chi-lites-i-like-your-lovin-do-.text:
I Like Your Lovin’ (Do You Like Mine) is the second studio album by The Chi-Lites. Eugene Record produced it and wrote most of it. It was released in 1970 on Brunswick. In discographies it counts as an original album, but there are only three new songs on it. The other seven come from the debut Give It Away.

Brunswick presumably chose this because the group had recorded too little new material by the time the title single came out. It was not a success: it is the group's only album on Brunswick that did not reach the top 100 on either chart. Are You My Woman? (Tell Me So), a modest hit at the time, later became one of their best-known songs. Its horn riff was heavily sampled in Beyoncé's Crazy in Love in 2003.
werk/the-chi-lites-i-like-your-lovin-do-.listen: Listen to Are You My Woman? (Tell Me So) and recognise the horn riff that Beyoncé sampled in Crazy in Love in 2003.

werk/the-clash-combat-rock.text:
Combat Rock is the fifth album by The Clash and was released in May 1982. After Sandinista!, Joe Strummer felt that the group was drifting creatively. Recording took place in London and at Electric Lady Studios in New York, and yielded eighteen songs. A quarrel arose between Strummer and Mick Jones over whether it should be a double album. Producer Glyn Johns cut the material down to a single record of twelve songs. Drummer Topper Headon was fired just before the release.

The music is post-punk and new wave, with influences of funk and reggae. The lyrics are about the Vietnam War, postcolonialism and the decay of American society. Straight to Hell tells of the children that American soldiers left behind in Vietnam. Rock the Casbah and Should I Stay or Should I Go became the best-known songs. The album became the group's best seller and its breakthrough in America, although some fans found the sound too radio-friendly.
werk/the-clash-combat-rock.listen: Listen to the slow, sombre atmosphere of Straight to Hell and notice how the lyrics tell a story without the music taking over the word.

werk/the-clash-cut-the-crap.text:
Cut the Crap is the sixth and last studio album by the Clash, released on 4 November 1985 on CBS. It was recorded in early 1985 at Weryton Studios near Munich, after Joe Strummer had fired guitarist Mick Jones and drummer Topper Headon. Manager Bernie Rhodes produced under the pseudonym Jose Unidos and fought with Strummer over the musical direction. Bassist Paul Simonon is not on the record: Norman Watt-Roy played the bass lines and a drum machine replaced drummer Pete Howard.

Rhodes chose synthetic drums and samples, which drew a lot of criticism. The press called the album one of the most disastrous records by a major artist. Strummer rejected it and disbanded the group within a few weeks. Even so critics praised his writing and singing, especially on This Is England, Dirty Punk and Three Card Trick.
werk/the-clash-cut-the-crap.listen: Listen to This Is England, the song the musicians agreed on, and notice how Strummer's voice relates to the electronic sounds.

werk/the-clash-give-em-enough-rope.text:
Give ’Em Enough Rope is the second studio album by the Clash, released on 10 November 1978 by CBS. It was the band's first album in the United States and the first with drummer Topper Headon. Sandy Pearlman produced. Joe Strummer played most of it on a rented Gibson ES-345, because his Telecaster was in for repair, and Pearlman mixed the drums louder than Strummer's vocals.

The lyrics deal with current topics. Tommy Gun is about aircraft hijackings, Julie's Been Working for the Drug Squad about the police action Operation Julie against an LSD ring in Wales, and Safe European Home about an uncomfortable trip by Strummer and Mick Jones to Jamaica. The album reached number 2 on the UK chart. Greil Marcus called it in Rolling Stone straightforward English punk with a grip on the future, and Sounds declared it record of the year.
werk/the-clash-give-em-enough-rope.listen: Listen to Safe European Home and notice the references to Jamaica, such as the Sheraton Hotel in Kingston.

werk/the-clash-london-calling.text:
After their second album, the Clash were stuck. There was a new manager, the old rehearsal room was gone and the writers Joe Strummer and Mick Jones had not made a new song for more than a year. In the summer of 1979 the band rehearsed shut off from the outside world at Vanilla Studios in Pimlico, at first with covers of rockabilly, rhythm and blues and reggae. From August they recorded the album at Wessex Sound Studios in London, in five to six weeks, with producer Guy Stevens.

It became a double album on which the punk sound opens out to reggae, rockabilly, ska, New Orleans R&B and lounge jazz. The lyrics are about unemployment, racial conflicts, drugs and the responsibilities of adulthood. London Calling reached the UK top ten and the title song became a top twenty single. The album is regarded as one of the best ever and in 2010 appeared on a British postage stamp.
werk/the-clash-london-calling.listen: Listen to The Guns of Brixton, bassist Paul Simonon's first song on an album by the band and the first on which he sang himself. Notice the reggae influence in the bass line.

werk/the-clash-sandinista.text:
Sandinista! was released on 12 December 1980 and was a triple album with 36 tracks. Recording took almost the whole year and took place in London, Manchester, Jamaica and New York. The band largely produced the record itself, with Bill Price as recording engineer. To be able to sell the album cheaply, the band gave up royalties on the first 200,000 copies sold in Great Britain.

The Clash went beyond punk and reggae and took in dub, rhythm and blues, calypso, gospel, jazz and rap. The influence of Lee Scratch Perry can be heard in the echoing, full sound. Washington Bullets is Joe Strummer's most outspoken political lyric up to that point. It is the only record on which all four members sing. Critics were at first critical of its size, but the record was later seen as an influential experiment.
werk/the-clash-sandinista.listen: Listen to Washington Bullets and notice how the lyrics name conflicts from different parts of the world.

werk/the-clash-the-clash.text:
The Clash is the British punk band's debut album, released on 8 April 1977 on CBS. The songs were largely written on the eighteenth floor of a tower block on Harrow Road in London, in a flat rented by Mick Jones's grandmother. Recording took three weeks in February 1977 and cost four thousand pounds. Mickey Foote, the group's sound engineer, produced. Drummer Terry Chimes played only on this album.

Joe Strummer and Jones wrote almost all the songs. Janie Jones is about a well-known London brothel keeper. Career Opportunities is about the lack of work. White Riot is short and intense, with a two-chord chorus, and is about class and race. Police and Thieves is a reggae cover. The album is musically varied for a punk band and reached number twelve in Great Britain. Later it appeared in many lists of the best punk albums.
werk/the-clash-the-clash.listen: Listen to White Riot and notice the chorus. It consists of two chords played very fast.

werk/the-cure-disintegration.text:
The album was released on 2 May 1989 and was The Cure's eighth. The band recorded it at Hook End in Oxfordshire, with co-producer David M. Allen. Singer Robert Smith was about to turn thirty and felt the pressure to make a more lasting work after the pop successes. He wanted to return to the sombre mood of the early 1980s, and the aftermath of the drugs he took can be heard in the sound. After the mixing sessions Smith threw the founder Lol Tolhurst out of the band.

The record company Elektra found the result deliberately incomprehensible, but Disintegration became the band's best-performing album up to that point. Lovesong reached number two on the American chart. The first reviews were warm, and later the album grew into a widely praised work. Since 2020 it has stood at number 116 in Rolling Stone's list of the five hundred best albums.
werk/the-cure-disintegration.listen: Listen to Lovesong, the biggest hit on the album. Notice how soft and intimate the song sounds compared with the despair that the rest of the record radiates.

werk/the-cure-pornography.text:
Pornography was released on 3 May 1982, as the band's fourth album. It was the first record with producer Phil Thornalley and was recorded from January to April at RAK Studios. The sessions were marked by a lot of drugs and quarrelling, and singer Robert Smith was deep in a depression. He thought it would be the group's last record. The album closed the dark period that had begun with Seventeen Seconds.

The music sounds dense, pounding and heavy. The NME reviewer called it Phil Spector in Hell. The Hanging Garden was the only song to be released as a single. Critics were not very enthusiastic when it came out, although the record entered at number eight in England. After that bassist Simon Gallup left the band and the group chose a lighter sound. Later Pornography received a lot of praise and is regarded as a landmark of gothic rock.
werk/the-cure-pornography.listen: Listen to The Hanging Garden, the only song on the album released as a single. Notice how dense and pounding the band sounds and how the vocals keep rising above it.

werk/the-cure-seventeen-seconds.text:
Seventeen Seconds is the second studio album by The Cure and was released on 18 April 1980 on Fiction Records. After the tour with Siouxsie and the Banshees, Robert Smith wanted a new direction. Bassist Michael Dempsey left, and Simon Gallup and keyboardist Matthieu Hartley joined. Smith worked with producer Mike Hedges. Because of a lack of money the record was recorded and mixed in seven days in January, with working days of sixteen or seventeen hours. As a result The Final Sound was cut down to 53 seconds, because the tape had run out.

The sound is sparse, echoing and sombre, with a drum sound that sets the direction. In retrospect the album is regarded as an early example of gothic rock. A Forest was the band's first single in the UK top 40. Critics called the lyrics vague and at times ominous and the melodies dark and minimalist. Nick Kent of NME thought The Cure sounded a good deal more mature on it.
werk/the-cure-seventeen-seconds.listen: Listen to A Forest and notice how the sparse, echoing sound creates a cold, ominous atmosphere.

werk/the-cure-the-head-on-the-door.text:
The Head on the Door is the sixth studio album by the Cure and was released on 30 August 1985 on Fiction Records. Drummer Boris Williams took part for the first time, and bassist Simon Gallup and guitarist Porl Thompson returned. It is the first record for which Robert Smith wrote all the songs alone and the first with several singles. Smith wanted, following the example of Kaleidoscope by Siouxsie and the Banshees, a varied record full of colours.

You can hear that. Kyoto Song has an oriental hook and The Blood is in flamenco style. In Between Days opens the album, and Close to Me was called a disco thing by critics. The title comes from the chorus of Close to Me. It became the band's first big international success, and Melody Maker chose it as best album of 1985.
werk/the-cure-the-head-on-the-door.listen: Listen to Close to Me, which critics called a disco thing, and compare its light tone with the opener In Between Days.

werk/the-cure-the-top.text:
The Top is the fifth studio album by the Cure and was released on 4 May 1984 on Fiction Records. Robert Smith wrote it during the period when he was also guitarist with Siouxsie and the Banshees. He worked with co-founder Lol Tolhurst, who had switched from drums to keyboards, and with new drummer Andy Anderson. All the songs are credited to Smith; three he wrote together with Tolhurst.

The style is eclectic, with violin and flute among other things. Bird Mad Girl has a Spanish atmosphere and Wailing Wall Middle Eastern influences. The Caterpillar was the only single. The British press was mostly positive, Melody Maker spoke of psychedelia that cannot be dated, but NME found the record self-satisfied. Later AllMusic called the record a necessary step in the band's development.
werk/the-cure-the-top.listen: Listen to Wailing Wall and notice the Middle Eastern undercurrent in the music.

werk/the-cure-three-imaginary-boys.text:
Three Imaginary Boys is The Cure's debut album, released on 8 May 1979 on Fiction Records. The producer was Chris Parry. The record company chose the songs, the running order and the sleeve without Robert Smith's permission. Since that album he has kept full creative control over every record. Smith himself was never satisfied. He found it quickly made and flat, and sometimes wrote lyrics while he was singing them. The album reached number 44 on the UK chart. In other countries it was later released under the title Boys Don't Cry with a different track list.

When it came out the reactions were good. Sounds gave it five stars and called Grinding Halt a pop song reminiscent of the Isley Brothers or the Buzzcocks. Later critics heard sharp post-punk and idiosyncratic pop, with an undertone of restrained melancholy. On Foxy Lady, a soundcheck, bassist Michael Dempsey sings.
werk/the-cure-three-imaginary-boys.listen: Listen to Foxy Lady and notice the singer: this is not Robert Smith but bassist Michael Dempsey. Can you hear how the recording sounds like a soundcheck?

werk/the-damned-machine-gun-etiquette.text:
On this third album from 1979 the band showed that punk could go in many directions. There are influences of hard rock, heavy metal and psychedelic rock, a touch of prog rock and even classic rhythm and blues from the 1960s. Journalists and fans described it as The Beach Boys meet Motörhead, with T. Rex and Judas Priest thrown in. There are also fast punk songs on it, and the record is regarded as a forerunner of hardcore punk.

The album opens with the voice of the actor Jack Howarth, taken from his album 'Ow Do with Lancashire monologues. There were guests: Joe Strummer sang along on Noise, Noise, Noise and clapped along on the title song. The cover shows the band on the street in New York. AllMusic wrote that when it came out the record was rightly seen as yet another classic by the group and praised the variety and the typical humour. Classic Rock later called it a wild, brazen race.
werk/the-damned-machine-gun-etiquette.listen: Listen to Smash It Up and notice the fast, bubbling punk that made the band so well known.

werk/the-damned-music-for-pleasure.text:
For The Damned's second album, in November 1977, a striking producer took the controls: Nick Mason of Pink Floyd. The band had first asked Syd Barrett, but he lived too withdrawn a life. Mason later said that the band was used to a much faster recording pace than he knew from Pink Floyd. A new guitarist took part, Lu Edmonds, alongside Brian James, and saxophonist Lol Coxhill played as a guest. It was the band's last studio record with James and the last on Stiff Records. The sleeve is by Barney Bubbles.

Musically the band remained punk, but the songs gained a more complicated structure. Problem Child was released beforehand as a single and did not make the official UK chart. The album did not either and was dismissed by critics at the time as a misstep. AllMusic later called it a respectable punk document.
werk/the-damned-music-for-pleasure.listen: Listen to Problem Child and notice how the band sounds: fast, raw and full of energy, as on the debut.

werk/the-damned-strawberries.text:
Strawberries was released in October 1982 on Bronze, at a time when the band was getting more attention thanks to Captain Sensible's solo success. During the recording, bassist Paul Gray and drummer Rat Scabies quarrelled over management and the writing of songs. Robert Fripp came by the studio, but their only joint song, Fun Factory, remained unreleased until 1990. The working title was Strawberries for Pigs. Singer Dave Vanian felt that playing new work for fans who only wanted to hear old songs was like giving strawberries to pigs.

The sound is melodic and varied, with sitar, cello and horns. Captain Sensible sings Life Goes On and Don't Bother Me. Vanian wrote The Dog about the vampire child Claudia from Anne Rice's Interview with the Vampire. Critics praised the musicianship and the influences from the 1960s, although NME called the album miserable at the time. It reached number 15, the band's first top 20 entry.
werk/the-damned-strawberries.listen: Listen to The Dog and notice how dark the story sounds in a song about the vampire child Claudia from Interview with the Vampire.

werk/the-damned-the-black-album.text:
In November 1980 a double album was released on Chiswick on which the punk band branched out into psychedelia. It was The Damned's fourth album and the first with bassist Paul Gray. The third side consists of a single track, Curtain Call. The fourth side contains live tracks, recorded at Shepperton Studios during a special concert for members of the fan club. Hans Zimmer co-produced The History of the World (Part 1).

Dave Vanian's vocals moved towards a darker side. Captain Sensible later said that it is just goth, although that was not the intention. Wait for the Blackout is regarded as a dramatic psych-punk outburst and 13th Floor Vendetta is a tribute to the film The Abominable Dr. Phibes. The album reached number 29 on the UK chart. Louder still calls it the group's psychedelic goth-punk high point.
werk/the-damned-the-black-album.listen: Listen to Wait for the Blackout and notice how the punk tempo goes together with dark, almost theatrical vocals.

werk/the-doors-l-a-woman.text:
The Doors' sixth studio album was released in April 1971 on Elektra and is the last with Jim Morrison in his lifetime. Producer Paul A. Rothchild dropped out after friction with the band and because he thought Love Her Madly was cocktail music. The group therefore produced the album itself, together with sound engineer Bruce Botnick. They set up an improvised studio in their rehearsal room on Santa Monica Boulevard, where Morrison sang in the bathroom doorway. Jerry Scheff, Elvis Presley's bassist, and guitarist Marc Benno played on it.

The album was finished in six days, with a raw, live sound and few overdubs. The blues influence is greater than ever. Morrison called the last session blues day, with Crawling King Snake and L.A. Woman among others. Love Her Madly reached the top 20 of the Billboard Hot 100. Critics see it as one of the group's best albums, because of Morrison's singing and the return to blues rock.
werk/the-doors-l-a-woman.listen: Listen to how raw and live the band sounds in L.A. Woman: the album was recorded with few overdubs.

werk/the-doors-other-voices.text:
Other Voices is the seventh studio album by the Doors and was released in October 1971 on Elektra Records. It was the first album after the death of singer Jim Morrison in July of that year. After the success of L.A. Woman, the three remaining members had begun recording while Morrison was staying in Paris. He died before he could return, and the others decided to carry on. Keyboardist Ray Manzarek and guitarist Robby Krieger shared the lead vocals.

Krieger later said that it was a hard time and that perhaps they should not have released the record so quickly, but that they did not sit around mourning and that Elektra wanted them to carry on. According to Jac Holzman the album sold about 300,000 copies. Record World called the single Tightrope Ride a smashing rocker that showed that the band could rock with other voices too. The record did not appear on CD until 2006.
werk/the-doors-other-voices.listen: Listen to Tightrope Ride, the single from the album, and notice how the band rocks without Jim Morrison as singer.

werk/the-doors-strange-days.text:
Strange Days is the second album by the Doors and was released on 25 September 1967 on Elektra Records, eight months after the debut. Recording ran in breaks between tours from February to August 1967 at Sunset Sound Recorders in Hollywood. Producer Paul A. Rothchild and sound engineer Bruce Botnick used a then new 8-track recorder and tried out all kinds of new recording techniques.

You can hear that in the instruments: from marimba to Moog synthesizer, one of the first times it was heard in rock. For Horse Latitudes, Botnick turned a tape recorder by hand to get a wind-like sound, while the band members played their instruments in unusual ways. The album closes with the eleven-minute When the Music's Over. It sold less than the debut, but the reactions were positive. One critic called it the group's own best-regarded work.
werk/the-doors-strange-days.listen: Listen to Horse Latitudes and notice the strange, wind-like sounds beneath Jim Morrison's spoken words. What do you think you are hearing: instruments or something else?

werk/the-doors-the-doors.text:
In the autumn of 1966 the group had been playing on the Sunset Strip in Los Angeles for some time. The Whisky a Go Go fired the band on 21 August, after singer Jim Morrison had improvised a passage from Oedipus Rex during The End. Elektra Records had signed the group three days earlier. Producer Paul A. Rothchild and sound engineer Bruce Botnick recorded the debut in about a month at Sunset Sound in Hollywood. What you hear on the record is, according to Botnick, what the band did live.

The album combines jazz, blues, classical, pop and R&B on a rock foundation, with organ and guitar at the core. Light My Fire became the breakthrough, in the full version, and The End closes with the spoken, improvised Oedipus section. The record was a commercial and critical success. In 2015 the Library of Congress included it in the National Recording Registry.
werk/the-doors-the-doors.listen: Listen to Light My Fire and notice Ray Manzarek's long organ solo and the guitar solo after it, which show how the group combines jazz and rock.

werk/the-doors-the-soft-parade.text:
The Soft Parade was released in July 1969 and was the fourth album by The Doors. After a gruelling tour there was little new material. Producer Paul Rothchild proposed a completely different approach: a fuller sound with horns and strings, arranged by Paul Harris. Jim Morrison was meanwhile struggling with personal problems and wrote less. Guitarist Robby Krieger took on a large part of the songs. Recording ran from November 1968 to May 1969 and made it the group's most expensive album.

Touch Me, with a saxophone solo by Curtis Amy, became one of the group's biggest hits. The title song begins with a mock sermon by Morrison and blends funk, jazz and psychedelia. Many listeners from the underground saw the horns and strings as a step towards pop. The criticism was harsh, and the record is still regarded as the weakest album with Morrison.
werk/the-doors-the-soft-parade.listen: Listen to Touch Me and notice the horns and strings, and the saxophone solo that appears later in the song.

werk/the-doors-waiting-for-the-sun.text:
Waiting for the Sun was the third album by The Doors and was released in July 1968. The group had already used most of the material from Jim Morrison's notebook on the first two records and was struggling with what drummer John Densmore called third-album syndrome. The recording, mainly at TTG Studios in Los Angeles, went with difficulty. Morrison's drinking caused tension and producer Paul Rothchild demanded countless takes. The long piece Celebration of the Lizard, intended for the second side, was dropped. Only the section Not to Touch the Earth made the record.

Hello, I Love You became the group's second number one in the United States. The Unknown Soldier, a reaction to the way the Vietnam War was shown on television, uses march rhythms and gunshots. Spanish Caravan shows Robby Krieger's flamenco guitar playing. The album received mixed reactions because of its variety, but it spent four weeks at the top of the Billboard 200 and is now judged more mildly.
werk/the-doors-waiting-for-the-sun.listen: Listen to The Unknown Soldier and notice the middle of the song, where you hear military commands and gunshots before the vocals return.

werk/the-everly-brothers-both-sides-of-a.text:
Both Sides of an Evening is the fifth studio album by The Everly Brothers and was released in 1961, at the peak of their career. Even so it did not reach any chart. The fourteen songs are arranged in two halves of seven: the first side was labelled for dancing, the second for dreaming. The producer was Bill Porter, and the sessions together lasted only three days. Guitarists such as Chet Atkins and Hank Garland played on it.

Before the release, half-minute excerpts from the songs appeared on a one-dollar Souvenir sampler. The album contains mostly older songs, such as My Mammy and Grandfather's Clock. A reviewer at AllMusic found it their most ambitious and mature record up to that point, but not very exciting for the teenagers who made up the bulk of their audience, certainly not the second side.
werk/the-everly-brothers-both-sides-of-a.listen: Listen to The Wayward Wind and notice how the two voices sound together and how calm the whole remains.

werk/the-everly-brothers-instant-party.text:
Instant Party! was released in 1962 and was recorded in Nashville between August and November 1961, shortly after Both Sides of an Evening. Like that predecessor, the album did not make the charts. The sleeve has an exclamation mark, the original label does not. Chet Atkins, Hank Garland and Floyd Cramer played on it.

The record consists mostly of older pop songs, such as Bye Bye Blackbird, True Love and Autumn Leaves. The brothers' usual rock 'n' roll sound is therefore almost entirely absent. AllMusic found the playing often impeccable, but incredibly boring on all but three songs, something the Everlys had never been before. The album was regarded as a low point in their artistic career.
werk/the-everly-brothers-instant-party.listen: Listen to Bye Bye Blackbird and notice how the two voices sing an old pop song: does it still sound like rock 'n' roll?

werk/the-everly-brothers-songs-our-daddy.text:
This second studio album by the Everly Brothers was released in 1958 on Cadence Records and consists of songs that the brothers had learned as boys from their father, Ike Everly. It is traditional music, released at the peak of their commercial success as a rock 'n' roll duo. Don and Phil play guitar and sing, Floyd Chance plays double bass. The accompaniment therefore stays extremely sparse.

That made the album unexpected. The music journalist Richie Unterberger called it ahead of its time, and The New Rolling Stone Album Guide wrote that even Elvis Presley would not have had the courage to make such a roots record. In January 1959 the album entered Cashbox's Best-Selling Pop Albums and reached number seventeen in three weeks. In 2013 Billie Joe Armstrong of Green Day and the singer Norah Jones made a version of their own under the title Foreverly.
werk/the-everly-brothers-songs-our-daddy.listen: Listen to the accompaniment on Roving Gambler: two guitars and a double bass, with no drums or orchestra, which puts the brothers' voices up front.

werk/the-ex-dignity-of-labour.text:
For this album the Dutch anarcho-punk band The Ex moved into an empty villa in Wormer. Nearby lay the Van Gelder paper factory, in the war a place of resistance against the German occupation and closed in 1980 after years of unsafe conditions, outdated machines and exploitation. The band wanted to honour the workers. With new drummer Sabien and producer Dolf Planteijdt, it recorded eight songs in his studio, supplemented with recordings in the abandoned factory itself.

The music has machine-like, industrial rhythms with engines, printing presses and pile drivers alongside guitar, double bass, drums, saxophone and marimba. The lyrics tell the life and death of the factory, from its founding in the nineteenth century to its takeover by an American multinational. The album came out as a box with four singles in blank black sleeves, with a booklet and a poster. The cover shows workers at the moment they heard the news of their dismissal.
werk/the-ex-dignity-of-labour.listen: Listen to Sucked Out Chucked Out 1 and notice the rhythms that sound like machines. Try to hear which sounds seem to come from the factory itself.

werk/the-ex-disturbing-domestic-peace.text:
Disturbing Domestic Peace is the debut album by The Ex, a Dutch anarchist band. The group formed in 1979, in the heyday of the squatters' movement. After the EP All Corpses Smell the Same the bassist left for New Zealand and the fifteen-year-old Bas took his place. In Dolf Planteijdt's studio they recorded ten songs about the Dutch housing shortage and squatting (Squatsong), police violence (Warning-Shot), environmental illness (A Sense of Tumour) and sexual violence (Meanwhile).

Because the studio material did not last half an hour, they pressed the record at 45 rpm and added a bonus single with four live tracks. The sleeve shows the police at the eviction of squatters. A lyric booklet was included, the beginning of a habit of putting a lot of extras in the sleeve. The first pressing of 1000 copies sold out within a week in October 1980.
werk/the-ex-disturbing-domestic-peace.listen: Listen to Squatsong and notice how short and direct the message about squatting is delivered.

werk/the-ex-history-is-what-s-happening.text:
History Is What's Happening was released in March 1982, two years after the Dutch punk band's debut. It contains songs that the group had played live in 1981, supplemented with material that came about in the studio. Recording began in the spray-painting room of the factory of the guitarist's uncle in Zaandam. Vocals and overdubs followed at the Koeienverhuur Studio, and by December 1981 everything was finished.

The twenty short songs are about Dutch domestic policy, the squatters' movement (Barricades), mechanisation on the shop floor (Machinery), government interference (Watch-Dogs) and the influence of the media on politics (Who Pays). A 24-page lyric booklet and a large poster were included. The sleeve shows a photograph of the Jewish orchestra in the Janowska concentration camp. The distributor had asked for 10,000 copies, but by the time the record came out the drummer had left. Performing was therefore impossible, and copies remained unsold for fifteen years.
werk/the-ex-history-is-what-s-happening.listen: Listen to Machinery, which lasts less than a minute, and notice how quickly the band makes its point about work and machines.

werk/the-four-tops-reach-out.text:
Reach Out was released in July 1967 and was the Four Tops' fifth studio album. It became their best-selling studio album and at the same time their last with the songwriting team Holland, Dozier and Holland. Six of their most successful singles are on it, including Reach Out I'll Be There, which reached number 1 in the United States and the United Kingdom, and Standing in the Shadows of Love, Bernadette and 7-Rooms of Gloom.

Besides their own hits there are covers of pop hits chosen by Berry Gordy, such as Tim Hardin's If I Were a Carpenter and the Left Banke's Walk Away Renée. These include two songs by the Monkees. Levi Stubbs sings the lead parts, the Funk Brothers play the accompaniment. BBC Music called the album a high point of Motown's first decade. In 2020 Rolling Stone put it at number 429 on its list of the 500 greatest albums ever.
werk/the-four-tops-reach-out.listen: Listen to Reach Out, I'll Be There and notice Levi Stubbs's voice: how does his singing build tension?

werk/the-four-tops-second-album.text:
Four Tops Second Album, also called simply Second Album, is the second studio album by the American R&B quartet, released on the label Motown. Most of the songs were written by the team Holland, Dozier and Holland. The album contains three hit singles. I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch) reached number 1 on both the black singles chart and the pop singles chart. It’s the Same Old Song reached 2 and 5, Something About You 9 and 19.

The record reached number 3 on Billboard's black albums chart and number 20 on the Top LPs. Levi Stubbs sings the lead on almost all the songs, the other three members provide the backing vocals, and the Funk Brothers supply the accompaniment. In 1990 Motown released the group's first two albums together on one CD.
werk/the-four-tops-second-album.listen: Listen to I Can't Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch) and notice how Levi Stubbs's lead vocal is complemented by the backing vocals of the other three members.

werk/the-human-league-crash.text:
Crash was released on 8 September 1986 on Virgin Records. After the slow work on its predecessor Hysteria, the band could not get going again and sessions with producer Colin Thurston ground to a halt. Virgin proposed working with the American production duo Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. In February 1986 the group travelled to Minneapolis. The duo replayed the parts by hand, so that according to the sleeve notes there are no sequencers on the album.

Towards the end a quarrel arose over who was boss in the studio, and singer Philip Oakey pulled the band back to Sheffield. Jam and Lewis finished their four songs themselves. The title comes from a crash cymbal: it was once again a disco record with lots of cymbals. Human became the band's second American number one. Keyboardist Philip Adrian Wright left the group afterwards.
werk/the-human-league-crash.listen: Listen to Human and notice the sound that Jam and Lewis gave it. According to the sleeve notes, no sequencers were used.

werk/the-human-league-dare.text:
At the end of 1980 the original line-up of the Human League fell apart. Philip Oakey and Philip Adrian Wright remained, added two teenage dancers and were deep in debt. At Virgin's insistence Oakey went to work with producer Martin Rushent in his studio in Berkshire. Recording ran from March to September 1981. The songs grew out of a simple Linn LM-1 rhythm, every note carefully chosen. Each track took about a week. Guitarist Jo Callis was the last to join.

The album moved from avant-garde electronic work to a more pop-oriented sound. Singles such as The Sound of the Crowd, Love Action and Open Your Heart preceded Don't You Want Me, a duet between Oakey and Susanne Sulley. He thought it the weakest song and therefore put it right at the end. It became the band's biggest hit and the Christmas single of 1981. The Musicians' Union condemned the record. Dare reached number one in England and is regarded as genre-defining.
werk/the-human-league-dare.listen: Listen to Don't You Want Me, the duet that comes last, and notice how the male and female voices alternate over the electronic accompaniment.

werk/the-human-league-hysteria.text:
Hysteria is the fourth studio album by the Human League, released on 7 May 1984 by Virgin Records. After the worldwide success of Dare in 1981, the group had trouble putting together a follow-up, and the recording went with difficulty. The title refers to that period. The producers Martin Rushent and Chris Thomas dropped out and Hugh Padgham finished the album.

The album reached number 3 in Great Britain and went gold, but fell short of its predecessor. Three singles reached the UK top 20, only The Lebanon made the American chart, at number 64. Rock Me Again and Again and Again and Again and Again and Again (Six Times) is a cover of a 1973 song by Lyn Collins and James Brown. I Love You Too Much is a heavily remixed version from the EP Fascination! and Don't You Know I Want You an adaptation of the instrumental B-side Total Panic!
werk/the-human-league-hysteria.listen: Listen to Don't You Know I Want You, which began as an instrumental B-side, and notice what role the vocals play in this song.

werk/the-human-league-romantic.text:
Romantic? was released in 1990 on Virgin Records and was the first album of new material in four years. Several producers worked on it, including Martin Rushent, who had helped the band on Dare and had walked away during Hysteria. Mark Brydon, later of Moloko, also produced a few songs. At that point the band was deep in a slump after the success of Dare nine years earlier.

That feeling comes through in The Stars Are Going Out, in which the band looks back on lost fame. The only real hit was the single Heart Like a Wheel, which reached number 29 in the United Kingdom. Soundtrack to a Generation followed as the second single. The album itself reached number 24. It was a commercial and critical low point, and Virgin ended the contract afterwards. For the next record the group switched to East West.
werk/the-human-league-romantic.listen: Listen to Heart Like a Wheel, the only real hit on the album, and notice how the song develops from beginning to end.

werk/the-human-league-travelogue.text:
Travelogue is the second album by the British synth-pop group The Human League, released in May 1980. It was the last with the founders Ian Craig Marsh and Martyn Ware, who left later that year to start Heaven 17. The band worked with a new co-producer, Richard Manwaring. Ware said that songs such as The Black Hit of Space were far ahead of their time: the synthesizers went through heavy distortion and overloaded the mixing desk.

The album reached number 16 on the UK chart. None of the singles, a new version of Being Boiled and a cover of Mick Ronson's Only After Dark, was a success. There is also a cover of the Gordon's Gin advertising jingle. When the group broke through in 1981 with a new line-up, the record re-entered the chart and went gold in 1982. In 2015 BBC 6Music devoted a documentary to it.
werk/the-human-league-travelogue.listen: Listen to The Black Hit of Space and notice the heavily distorted, overdriven synthesizers.

werk/the-impressions-keep-on-pushing.text:
Keep On Pushing was released in 1964 on ABC-Paramount and is The Impressions' most successful album. It reached number 8 on the Billboard 200 and number 4 on the R&B chart. Curtis Mayfield's title song reached number 10 on the Hot 100 and topped the R&B chart.

Johnny Pate wrote the horn arrangements, and the smooth harmony singing gives the album its colour. For Amen, Mayfield took inspiration from the film Lilies of the Field, in which Jester Hairston sang the spiritual. In the studio they began with a swing low sweet chariot and moved into a march-like rhythm. On the sleeve the trio is pushing Mayfield's Jaguar. The album can be seen on the cover of Bob Dylan's Bringing It All Back Home, and Bob Marley included Amen and I Made a Mistake in the Wailers' regular setlist. In 2017 Pitchfork put it at number 167 of the best albums of the 1960s.
werk/the-impressions-keep-on-pushing.listen: Listen to Amen and notice how the spiritual is transformed into a soul song with a march-like rhythm and communal singing.

werk/the-isley-brothers-shout.text:
Shout! is the Isley Brothers' debut album, released in 1959 on RCA Victor. Hugo Peretti and Luigi Creatore produced it. After the success of the title song the group was sent hurriedly into the studio to record a large part of the record. That included Respectable, a second song that was later covered by rock bands, although it did not itself reach any chart.

Ronald Isley sings the lead parts, while O'Kelly Jr. and Rudolph Isley do the backing vocals. When the album had long been out of print, it was reissued in 1990 on Collectables. In 2015 it was included in an expanded, remastered version in a CD box set of RCA Victor and T-Neck recordings.
werk/the-isley-brothers-shout.listen: Listen to the lead vocals and the backing vocals in Shout and notice how they alternate.

werk/the-isley-brothers-soul-on-the-rock.text:
Soul on the Rocks is the fifth studio album by the Isley Brothers and was released on 29 August 1967 on Tamla, Motown's label in Detroit. It was their second and last record there. The brothers became disappointed with their time at Motown. Groups such as the Temptations and the Four Tops, who sounded slicker than the Isleys, received more promotion.

One of the songs, Behind a Painted Smile, did well on the charts. It made the group popular in the United Kingdom, which the brothers noticed when they toured the country in that period. That gave them new courage. Shortly afterwards they left Motown and re-established their own label, T-Neck. The album thus marks the end of a short, disappointing period.
werk/the-isley-brothers-soul-on-the-rock.listen: Listen to Behind a Painted Smile and notice how the vocals carry the pain in the lyrics, while the accompaniment stays polished.

werk/the-isley-brothers-twisting-and-sho.text:
Twisting and Shouting was released in 1963 on United Artists and was the third album by the Isley Brothers, here billed as the Famous Isley Brothers. A year earlier Twist & Shout had come out. None of the songs reached the singles charts. Alan Lorber and Garry Sherman conducted.

After that it stayed quiet for three years. The next album, This Old Heart of Mine from 1966, was released on Berry Gordy's Motown. Ronald Isley sang the lead parts, his brothers O'Kelly Jr. and Rudolph sang along in the background. In 1991 the record came out on CD with extra tracks, under the title The Complete United Artists Sessions.
werk/the-isley-brothers-twisting-and-sho.listen: Listen to Ronald Isley's lead vocal in Long Tall Sally and notice the energy with which he sings the song.

werk/the-jackson-5-abc.text:
This second album by the Jackson 5 was released on 8 May 1970 on Motown, less than six months after their debut. It contains the number 1 singles ABC and The Love You Save, and the album reached the top four of the American pop albums and number one on the R&B albums chart. The musicians who played the songs were not credited at the time, because Motown only began naming session musicians from 1971.

Besides the hits there are striking album tracks: a cover of Funkadelic's I'll Bet You, the song The Young Folks, previously recorded by Diana Ross and the Supremes, and I Found That Girl, the only song with Jermaine as lead singer. AllMusic called it perhaps the brothers' strongest album of the early 1970s. The title song was nominated for a Grammy Award. The album is regarded as one of the group's most popular records.
werk/the-jackson-5-abc.listen: Listen to ABC and notice how the young lead singer and his brothers' harmonies make the song so playful and tight.

werk/the-jackson-5-christmas-album.text:
Christmas Album was released on 15 October 1970 on Motown and was the Jackson 5's fourth studio album and first Christmas album. It closed a successful year in which the group released three albums. The Corporation and Hal Davis produced it.

The group gave well-known Christmas songs a modern twist. Santa Claus Is Coming To Town was released as a single, and together with I Saw Mommy Kissing Santa Claus it is still played on the radio every year at Christmas time. Michael Jackson and Jermaine Jackson share the lead vocals. In December 1970 the record spent four weeks at the top of Billboard's special Christmas chart. Critics called the album one of the best Christmas records. Rolling Stone spoke of a gem, and AllMusic gave it four and a half stars.
werk/the-jackson-5-christmas-album.listen: Listen to Santa Claus Is Coming To Town and notice how an old Christmas song sounds here like a Motown pop song.

werk/the-jackson-5-diana-ross-presents-t.text:
This debut album was released on 12 December 1969 on Motown. The title made it sound as if Diana Ross had discovered the group, and she even wrote the text on the back. That was a marketing plan by the label. In reality producer Bobby Taylor had found the brothers, and Gladys Knight too said that she had brought them to Motown's attention. Ross, however, gladly took on the role and helped to promote the group.

Recording ran from May to August 1969. The record consists of twelve songs, with the still very young Michael Jackson as lead singer alongside his brothers Jackie, Tito, Jermaine and Marlon. It is tight harmony singing with a lot of youthful energy and a funky undertone, as AllMusic described it. The only single, I Want You Back, was at number 1 on the American Hot 100 within a few weeks. Critics were very positive and saw in the album the beginning of a new era in crossover pop and soul.
werk/the-jackson-5-diana-ross-presents-t.listen: Listen to I Want You Back and notice how Michael takes the lead while his brothers follow him with short, tight voices.

werk/the-jackson-5-third-album.text:
Third Album was released on 8 September 1970 on Motown. It was the Jackson 5's third studio album, produced by The Corporation and Hal Davis.

The most important song is I'll Be There, the group's fourth consecutive number one on the American pop chart. Mama's Pearl also became a big hit. The album also includes Goin' Back to Indiana, a semi-autobiographical song, and Darling Dear. The record stayed close to the familiar Motown sound and left just enough room for other influences. AllMusic gives the album four out of five stars. It is regarded as one of the group's best records. In 2001 it was released on CD together with Maybe Tomorrow.
werk/the-jackson-5-third-album.listen: Listen to I'll Be There and notice how the vocals carry the song, with the band as a calm backdrop.

werk/the-jimi-hendrix-experience-axis-bo.text:
Axis: Bold as Love was released in December 1967, only seven months after the successful debut Are You Experienced. The Jimi Hendrix Experience recorded it at Olympic Studios in London, with Chas Chandler as producer and Eddie Kramer as sound engineer. Just before the end of recording Hendrix left the master of the first side in a taxi, after which the trio remixed the songs in a single night. Hendrix was afterwards not satisfied with that haste.

The album shows various musical styles, and critics saw in it Hendrix's growth as a songwriter. Spanish Castle Magic and Little Wing come from his past with rhythm-and-blues bands and stayed in his live repertoire throughout his career. On If 6 Was 9 he also plays recorder. The sleeve, with Hindu imagery, caused a stir, and Hendrix said publicly that he did not agree with it. The record was a critical and commercial success.
werk/the-jimi-hendrix-experience-axis-bo.listen: Listen to the guitar playing in Little Wing and to how soft and restrained the song sounds.
